tagline.text: A quiet cove ringed by red hills, the farthest in San Antonio

location.label: Location
location.text: San Antonio, Zambales; the farthest cove reached by boat from Pundaquit

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,500 (per person, based on a day tour with a boat shared by 4)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: Silanguin Cove is the farthest of the coves you reach by boat along the San Antonio coast in Zambales. Unlike Anawangin and Nagsasa, it has gray sand, and its quiet beach ringed by reddish hills is good for swimming and camping.

Silanguin Cove lies at the southern end of the string of secluded coves along the coastline of San Antonio, Zambales. Travel blogs and local guides describe this stretch as a set of recently rediscovered hidden beaches, and they single out Silanguin as the farthest and quietest. The Wikipedia entry for San Antonio spells the name "Silangen Cove," so the spelling varies a little. Local boat operators and travel guides mostly say Silanguin or Silanguin Cove, so it helps to know both spellings when you book.

What sets this cove apart from its neighbors Anawangin and Nagsasa is the sand. Anawangin and Nagsasa are dark gray beaches covered in ash from the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption, while Silanguin is described as having light gray sand. One travel guide wrote that it is less striking to look at than the neighboring coves but that the surrounding scenery makes up for it. Reddish hills enclose the cove, and the water is relatively shallow with gentle waves, which are counted as advantages for swimming. People who want somewhere calm when Anawangin and Nagsasa are crowded with campers choose Silanguin.

The basic way in is by boat from Pundaquit. Because it is the farthest from Pundaquit, the boat fare is also the highest among the coves, and one travel guide listed the combined Silanguin, Capones and Camara trip as the most expensive. You can also come by boat from the Subic side, but that takes longer. No overland walking route is known, so assume you reach it almost entirely by boat. Getting to Pundaquit means taking a bus from Manila toward Iba or Santa Cruz, getting off in front of the San Antonio market, and continuing by tricycle.

This guide is for travelers who leave Manila and spend a day or a night out of Pundaquit looking for a quiet cove. There is not much up-to-date information on Silanguin. Much of the fee and facility information confirmed so far comes from blogs dated around 2014–2020, so be sure to recheck entrance fees, boat fares and whether the lodging is available with a Pundaquit boat operator or the San Antonio tourism office. Bearing in mind that facilities are limited, bring food, water and trash bags with you, which is the best way to enjoy this cove properly. Note also that the trek from Pundaquit over the mountain to Anawangin Cove is said to take about 4–5 hours, but no walking route to Silanguin has ever been described, so plan your trip on the assumption that you will go by boat.

Unlike the dark volcanic ash sand of Anawangin and Nagsasa, this cove has light gray sand. It does not blow around like dust the way ash beaches do, so your feet stay cleaner. Comparing the sand colors in photos is part of the fun.

The hills behind the cove have a reddish tint that gives it a different feel from the other coves. One guide judged that this scenery makes up for the beach's plain looks. The red looks sharper in the light of early morning and late afternoon.

The water is said to be shallower and the waves weaker than at other coves, which makes swimming pleasant. It is comparatively reassuring with children or weak swimmers, but always wear a life jacket. Depth differs from beach to beach, so ask your guide before you get in.
There is a place at the cove that rents accommodation. An older guide listed a two-room hut at
per night. That rate dates from about 2014–2018, so check current rates and how to book directly.
Some Pundaquit boat owners also run fishing tours. If you tell them in advance they will prepare fishing gear, so ask when you book the boat if you want to fish during your Silanguin visit.

blocks.title: A boat route combined with Capones and Camara

children.text: Silanguin Cove is usually visited on a route that also takes in the Capones Island lighthouse and Camara Island. After swimming at the cove, you see the lighthouse and the rocky island on the way back. Because one boat covers three stops, you get a lot to see for the cost.

The coves of San Antonio are known as camping spots, and camping is recommended at Silanguin too. Travelers say that with little light from the city at night, the stars show up well. You must bring all your equipment, food and water, and carry your trash back out.
Leave Manila early, take a bus to the San Antonio market, and continue to Pundaquit by tricycle.
In Pundaquit pay the environmental fee and take a boat to Silanguin Cove. It is the farthest cove, so the ride takes a long time.
On arrival pay the entrance fee, then swim on the beach and have lunch.
Take the boat to Capones Island and climb the lighthouse.
Return to Pundaquit via Camara Island.
Watch the sunset in Pundaquit, then go out to San Antonio and check the time of the last bus to Manila.
Silanguin is the farthest stop, so a day trip is tight. If your schedule allows, stay the night before in Pundaquit and set out early in the morning.
Travel to Pundaquit, have lunch, and buy the water and food you need.
Take a boat to Silanguin and pitch a tent or put your bags in a hut.
Cook dinner on the beach and watch the stars. Check the rules on fires first.
Get up early, stroll the beach, swim, then take the boat back to Pundaquit.
Take a bus from San Antonio back to Manila.
Settle the boat's return time in advance. You can also ask about sharing the return boat.
Take a Victory Liner bus to Iba or Santa Cruz and get off in front of the San Antonio Public Market. Fares vary widely between guides, from ₱250 to ₱400.
Take a tricycle from the market to Pundaquit. The fare is given as about ₱30–40 per person.
In Pundaquit, find an early boat to Silanguin Cove.
The trip from Manila to San Antonio is said to take about 4–5 hours.
Hire a bangka (small boat) at Pundaquit Beach. The fare is per boat, and a boat usually carries about 4 people.
The Silanguin, Capones and Camara route cost about ₱2,500 in older guides and has risen to ₱3,000 in some later price lists.
You can also come by boat from Subic, but it takes longer than from Pundaquit.
To reach Pundaquit, enter "Pundaquit Beach" in Google Maps.
Cars cannot reach the cove, so you must take a boat from Pundaquit.

Silanguin Cove is most dependable in the dry season from November to May. In this period the seas are calm and boats reach the farthest cove easily. In the rainy season boats to the farthest coves are the first affected, so build spare weather days into your plan from June to October.

San Antonio receives about 1,280 mm of rain a year, with most falling from June to September. Anawangin and Nagsasa fill up on weekends, but Silanguin is said to be relatively quiet, and a weekday is quieter still.

Camping is the most recommended way to stay at Silanguin Cove. A guide once said Puerto Silanguin rents out huts, but the exact facilities and rates may change over time. If you want a comfortable bed, you can stay at a resort in Pundaquit and make a day tour out of it.

Prepare as if there is almost nowhere to buy food. Buy rice, meat, vegetables and water at Pundaquit or the San Antonio market and carry them in. Other coves are said to allow your own grill or portable stove, but the rules at Silanguin need to be confirmed.

It helps to look at the rates of the neighboring coves when estimating costs. One travel guide listed a boat to Anawangin only at about ₱1,000, a boat to Nagsasa only at about ₱1,500, and a boat combining Silanguin, Capones and Camara at about ₱2,500, and it gave the Anawangin overnight fee as ₱100 per person and Nagsasa Falls entry as ₱30. All of these figures are from old sources, so use only the general point that Silanguin, being the farthest, costs more by boat than the neighboring coves, and settle exact amounts on site. Besides boat operators, some places in Pundaquit village let you use a shower with a resort day pass, so it is also good to find out in advance where you can wash up after you return.
The cove is the farthest, so the boat ride is long; leave room in your schedule. If possible, start early in the morning.
Boat fares are often quoted per boat, so splitting it among 4 people lowers the cost.
Much of the information on entrance and hut fees is old, so ask the boat operator ahead of time.
Bring plenty of water, food and trash bags, and carry out all your trash.
Use reef-safe sunscreen and a reusable water bottle.
If you want to fish, tell the operator when you book the boat so they can prepare fishing gear.
Dogs or livestock may be on the beach at the cove, so do not leave food unattended.
In the rainy season and during typhoons, boats to the farther coves may not go out. Check the weather and whether boats are running before you leave.
Always wear a life jacket and keep to the boat's passenger limit.
Silanguin is remote, so it takes a long time to reach a hospital in an emergency. Bring basic medicines and emergency contacts.
Mobile signal may be weak, so decide on offline maps and a way to stay in touch in advance.
Information on facilities and rates comes from old sources, so be sure to confirm the latest on site.
Do not leave trash behind or touch plants and coral, so as not to harm the natural environment.
